<reason>Side A owned the debate's central question from the opening: if conduct is stipulated lawful and job-irrelevant, may a worker be fired on pure disapproval? A then turned B's best weapons. The Rebuttal 1 catch that B1.1's absolute exit-right contradicts B1.5's praised targeted statutes forced B onto a narrow-vs-boundless defense, and A's proves-too-much answer to the pretext/contractor evasion argument (it would void the very discrimination laws B endorses) was never squarely rebutted. B's strongest late move — the prospective-risk gambling bookkeeper — was dismantled in A's closing: a forecast-of-offense principle has no limiting principle and can rationalize any firing, while genuinely demonstrable risk already qualifies as material. B's closing reply ("discrimination is already illegal") missed the point for the unprotected territory B's own opening admitted exists, and B's pivot to severance/unemployment insurance read as cushioning arbitrary power rather than justifying it. B landed real pressure on the vagueness of "materially" and small-business litigation costs, keeping the debate competitive, and both sides stayed epistemically clean with compliant Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formats; the mutual clipped turns and A's slightly cheap chronological jab about B's "silence" were minor. Overall A made the decisive clashes clearer and gave the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1: the contradiction catch between B's absolute exit-right (B1.1) and its endorsed narrow statutes (B1.5), combined with turning B's "paper the file" pretext scenario into a confession — under the status quo the worker has zero recourse, while under the motion pretext is at least contestable ("a right sometimes evaded still beats a right that does not exist"). B never fully recovered the initiative after that exchange.</best_rebuttal>
